question: What does Morgan Stanley pay its financial advisors?

claims.text: MS: The 2025 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025) states that for certain revenue-producing employees in the Wealth Management and Investment Management business segments, compensation is largely paid on the basis of formulaic payouts that link employee compensation to revenues.

MS: The 1Q26 10-Q (period ended March 31, 2026) and 2Q26 10-Q (period ended June 30, 2026) state that deferred compensation for financial advisors in the Wealth Management business segment is generally composed of 75% cash-based awards and 25% stock-based awards.

MS: The 2Q26 10-Q (period ended June 30, 2026) states that in the first quarter of 2026, Morgan Stanley reduced the amount of deferred compensation as a proportion of total compensation for Wealth Management advisors.

MS: On the 4Q25 earnings call (January 2026), Morgan Stanley announced it will increase the cash component of its advisor compensation, describing these changes as supporting its overall investment into its financial advisors.

MS: Trade press reports (October 2026) that Morgan Stanley is increasing a pay threshold for advisors by 10% in 2027, meaning advisors have to generate that much more revenue to see the same pay next year.

MS: Trade press reports (October 2026) that Morgan Stanley and Merrill Lynch are not introducing retention bonuses as part of their 2027 pay plans for advisors, adhering to a more traditional approach.

MS: Trade press reports (October 2026) that firms like Morgan Stanley have for years taken a small amount of an advisor's gross revenue, called it deferred compensation, and required advisors to stay for years in order to vest.

MS: The 1Q26 10-Q (period ended March 31, 2026) states that compensation expense for deferred cash-based compensation (DCP) awards is calculated based on the notional value of the award granted, adjusted for changes in the fair value of the referenced investments that employees select, and is recognized over the vesting period relevant to each separately vesting portion of deferred awards.

MS: The 1Q26 10-Q (period ended March 31, 2026) states that employees are permitted to allocate the value of their deferred cash-based awards among a menu of notional investments selected by the Firm, which includes fixed income, equity, commodity and money market funds.

MS: The 2025 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025) states that compensation and benefits expenses include base salaries and fixed allowances, formulaic programs, discretionary incentive compensation, amortization of deferred cash and equity awards, changes in the fair value of referenced notional DCP investments, carried interest allocated to employees, severance costs, and other items such as health and welfare benefits.

MS: Wealth Management segment compensation expense (which includes financial advisors and other Wealth Management employees) was $16,950 million in fiscal 2025, compared with $15,207 million in fiscal 2024, per the January 15, 2026 press release.
MS: Wealth Management segment compensation expense was $4,860 million in 3Q 2026, compared with $4,388 million in 3Q 2025, per the October 14, 2026 press release.

MS: Trade press reports (October 2026) that Morgan Stanley is increasing a pay threshold for financial advisors by 10% in 2027, meaning advisors must generate that much more revenue to receive the same pay next year.
MS: Trade press reports (October 2026) that Morgan Stanley is not introducing retention bonuses as part of its 2027 pay plan for advisors, adhering to a more traditional approach.

MS: The 2025 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025) states that for certain revenue-producing employees in the Wealth Management segment, compensation is largely paid on the basis of formulaic payouts that link employee compensation to revenues.

MS: The 1Q26 10-Q (period ended March 31, 2026) states that deferred compensation for financial advisors in the Wealth Management business segment is generally composed of 75% cash-based awards and 25% stock-based awards.

MS: On the 4Q25 earnings call (January 2026), Morgan Stanley stated it will increase the cash component of its advisor compensation, announced alongside the transition of DCP hedges to derivative instruments.

MS: The 2Q26 10-Q (period ended June 30, 2026) states that its deferred cash-based and stock-based compensation programs for current and former employees, including financial advisors in Wealth Management, generally contain vesting, clawback and cancellation provisions.

MS: The 3Q25 10-Q (period ended September 30, 2025) states that Wealth Management advisor compensation includes a formulaic (production/revenue-based) payout, as higher compensation expense was driven by an increase in the formulaic payout to Wealth Management advisors on higher revenues.

MS: The 2025 10-K states that compensation and benefits expenses (firmwide) include base salaries and fixed allowances, formulaic programs, discretionary incentive compensation, amortization of deferred cash and equity awards, changes in fair value of referenced notional DCP investments, carried interest, severance costs and other items such as health and welfare benefits.

MS: The 2Q26 10-Q (period ended June 30, 2026) states that in the first quarter of 2026 the Firm reduced the amount of deferred compensation as a proportion of total compensation for Wealth Management advisors.

MS: Trade press reports (October 2026) that Morgan Stanley is increasing a pay threshold for advisors by 10% in 2027, and is not introducing retention bonuses as part of its 2027 pay plans for advisors.

MS: On the 4Q25 earnings call (January 2026), Morgan Stanley announced it will increase the cash component of advisor compensation, a change it said supports its investment in financial advisors and helps simplify its compensation program. Why it might matter: the source states these changes are being made to reduce the accounting-driven volatility in revenues and earnings.

MS: The 2Q26 10-Q (period ended June 30, 2026) states that beginning in the first quarter of 2026, Morgan Stanley reduced the amount of deferred compensation as a proportion of total compensation for Wealth Management advisors. Why it might matter: the source notes that beginning in the first quarter of 2026 the Firm reduced deferred compensation as a proportion of total compensation, a change from prior practice.

MS: The 2Q26 10-Q (period ended June 30, 2026) states that beginning in the first quarter of 2026, Morgan Stanley primarily transitioned hedges for Wealth Management DCP awards to derivative instruments. Why it might matter: the 1Q26 press release reported Wealth Management segment total Compensation expense of $4,648 million for the first quarter of 2026, the same period the transition began.

MS: Trade press reports (October 2026) that Morgan Stanley is increasing a pay threshold for advisors by 10% in 2027, meaning advisors have to generate that much more revenue to see the same pay next year. Why it might matter: the source states that as it has in the past, Morgan Stanley is increasing a pay threshold for advisors by 10% in 2027.

MS: Trade press reports (October 2026) that Morgan Stanley is not introducing retention bonuses as part of its 2027 pay plan for advisors, adhering to a more traditional approach. Why it might matter: the source notes that Morgan Stanley is increasing a pay threshold for advisors by 10% in 2027, while Merrill Lynch is leaving its core pay plan for advisors unchanged for next year.
